stimulus.text: The United Nations Charter, signed in June 1945, gave the five great powers — including the United States — a veto in the Security Council, so no Council action could pass over an American veto. In 1919 the Senate had rejected the League of Nations, fearing that membership would drag the United States into foreign wars.

stem: Why did the United States join the United Nations after rejecting the League of Nations in 1919?

options.text: The Charter gave the United Nations command of the American army
options.misconception: The United States kept command of its own forces; the Charter gave the United Nations no standing army.

options.text: The Charter protected American freedom of action through the veto
The Charter banned the United States from ever using force
options.misconception: The Charter allowed force to keep the peace; it did not ban the use of force.

options.text: The Charter required every nation to join the League first
options.misconception: The League of Nations was gone by 1945, and no nation had to join it first.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the United States kept command of its own forces; the Charter gave the United Nations no standing army.
rationales.B: The veto meant the United Nations could never order the United States into action against its will, which answered the Senate's fear from 1919 that membership would drag America into foreign wars.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the Charter allowed force to keep the peace; it did not ban the use of force.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the League of Nations was gone by 1945, and no nation had to join it first.
rationales.general:
1. The Charter gave the great powers a veto in the Security Council.
2. Background: in 1919 the Senate had rejected the League, fearing it would drag the United States into foreign wars.
3. The veto changed that fear: no Council action could pass over an American veto.
4. The lesson of the 1930s also mattered: staying out had not kept America safe from war.
Remember: a nation joins an organization when it trusts the rules to protect its own freedom to choose.
